We are so glad you joined us.

Regen Commons
It’s a decentralized brand and IP commons designed to nurture & grow the Regen identity across Web3, ensuring it remains a public good while aligning shared incentives.

Here are some things you can do to get started:
 Introduce yourself by adding your picture and information about yourself and your interests to your profile. What is one thing you’d like to be asked about?
 Get to know the community by browsing discussions that are already happening here. When you find a post interesting, informative, or entertaining, use the  to show your appreciation or support!

If you need help or have a suggestion, feel free to ask in Site Feedback or contact the admins.

# .regen onchain AI agents — tooling offer for Regen Commons


## Post 1 by tmo
*2025-07-15T21:54:31.414Z*

Excited to see Gaia AI and Regen Network AI Agent Collab!
Context
With Gaia and Regen teaming up on agent infrastructure, it seems like the right time to officially contribute the .regen onchain agent contract to Regen Commons. The contract already runs in production for other namespaces and is designed to be handed over to and operated by the steward of your choice; it is fully decentralized.

What the contract provides




Feature
Notes




Unique onchain agent names
alice.regen, foundation.regen, plot-42.regen, etc.


Soul-bound identity
Each name has its own cross-chain 0x wallet (ERC-20, 721, 1155, signing, approvals) with full agent identity (bio, purpose, mandate, place, style)


Modular control
Manual (owner wallet), automated (program), or autonomous (LLM via ElizaOS).


Client-agnostic
Works with our two front-ends, other open-source dashboards, or any custom client you build.


DeFi ready
Live swaps and transfers; Aave, Uni LP, Farcaster MiniApp, NLP Tx creation in the queue.


Fundraising
Name creation can be permissioned or permissionless; free or priced; use priced account creation to raise funds for Regen Commons




Design space for Regen Commons with .regen agents

Governance hooks (token-weighted, reputation-based, or both).
Place-based and impact metrics.
Treasury automations (market-making, reward flows, grant disbursements).
Reputation or credential overlays.
ElizaOS: use ours or install plugin on yours; use any LLM

Happy to collaborate on any of the above. All collabs from any group are open source for all groups to use.

Relation to natural capital ensurance by BASIN

Ensurance is markets for what matters; primarily built to ensure natural capital.  Ensurance links stocks (ERC-1155 assets) and flows (ERC-20 currencies) to fund natural assets and the people who care for them.
A namespace (ie .regen) is a Group contract.
Agent accounts are part of that namespace and can designate a primary currency/asset to focus their efforts.
Polycentric All groups and agents operate independently but benefit from collective activity called ensurance proceeds.


Next steps

Express interest—reply here or DM.
Allow-list—I’ll add interested parties so they can mint their accounts.
Live demo—walk-through with real agent accounts.
Hand-off / Stewardship transfer—contract ownership passes to the entity the community designates (Regen Commons, Regen Foundation, RND, etc.).

Current footprint: 25 other namespaces, \800+ agent accounts. The architecture scales indefinitely.

Contact
We have a small Telegram chat going re this, or happy to schedule a call / Twitter Space / video if that’s easier. Let me know how you’d like to proceed.
I really think this could be a useful tool for the Regen movement and excited to hand-it off to you.

## Post 2 by m3metix
*2025-03-21T05:10:19.805Z*

I see this as a well intentioned approach here. But is it attempting to protect regenerative values and the expression of these in our work as mirrors of living systems using the very mechanisms of extraction and control that regenerative systems seek to transform? Maybe there is good creative tension in all this. But I honestly think it’s a suck on energy and attention. What is being protected here? Like creating all these bureaucratic and technocratic mechanisms when the energy could be better devoting to creating healing relationships with our kin.
Know that this comes from a genuine place of care but I just think and feel this whole approach is not attuned to the regenerative spirit at the basis of our work. You cannot trademark or own being in right relationship with Earth’s systems. That relationship exists through practice, presence, and participation. I understand the fear of co-opting that is happening and will continue to happen but is this whole approach a diversion?


## Post 3 by guil
*2025-04-03T18:08:15.774Z*

I agree. This isn’t meant to become a big bureaucracy or drain anyone’s energy.
If you check the proposal, you’ll see it’s designed to be as minimal as possible: the word ‘regen initiative’ stays open for anyone, and if there’s a problem, we try to address it socially first, only going the legal route if absolutely necessary.
We just don’t want what happened with ‘Sustainable’ (where it got co-opted and lost all meaning) to happen again. Greenwashing is real, and it hurts people doing the real work.

## Post 1 by Gregory0
*2025-04-01T16:58:37.164Z*

Regen Commons Facilitation RFP
Co-Designing the Constitution for a Decentralized Brand Commons

 Overview
Regen Commons is initiating a facilitation-led process to co-create its governance, legal, and economic architecture. This RFP invites qualified facilitators or facilitator collectives to manage a participatory process that culminates in a foundational constitution or organizing document.
This is a pivotal moment to build legitimacy within the regenerative Web3 ecosystem by aligning legal structures, governance mechanisms, and memetic power around the Regen identity.

 Goals
The selected facilitator(s) will manage a structured, inclusive process to define and document:

Legal Framework

Structure and purpose of the Commons (e.g., Purpose Trust, DUNA)


Governance Mechanism

Decision-making rules, onboarding, voting models


Token Strategy

Use, issuance, rights, and responsibilities


Membership Model

How new members are added and recognized


Contribution Valuation

How to assess and reward new contributions (e.g. IP, labor, capital)


Exit Mechanism

Offboarding protocols and exit options


Business Plan & Relationship to SporkDAO

Funding roadmap, governance alignment, and SporkDAO participation




 Target Audience
The resulting process and documents should resonate with and gain legitimacy from the Web3 regenerative community, including:

ReFi founders & contributors
DAO governance experts
Decentralized identity and public goods advocates
Projects using the “Regen” brand/meme


 Deliverables

Facilitation of a multi-phase engagement (e.g. workshops, async input, synthesis)
Final draft of a Regen Commons Constitution / Core Document
A public-facing summary for community ratification
Implementation roadmap & recommendations


 Evaluation Criteria

Track record in Web3 governance, legal design, and facilitation
Familiarity with regenerative economics and ReFi principles
Experience distilling group complexity into actionable frameworks
Ability to manage time-sensitive, high-integrity processes
Alignment with Regen Commons values


 Budget & Timeline

Budget: $20,000
Timeline: May–June 2025 (Deliverables complete)
Funding: Seed funding from SporkDAO, with follow on and complimentary funding from Regen Network, and other Regen Commons members possible.


 Invited Candidates


Jessica Zartler / BlockScience Team
(Systemic governance + crypto-economic modeling expertise)


Regen Unite (Cori + collaborators)
(Deeply involved in framing Regen Commons narrative and organizing early sessions)


Open Civics (Benjamin Life, Jess, Sam)
(Sense-making methodology, ontological document design, multi-org consensus-building)


You?
Submit your proposal to join this shortlist.



 Governance & Selection
Proposals will be reviewed by a multi-sig committee composed of:

Gregory Landua
Kevin Owocki
Griff Green
Michael Zargham
Scott Moriss
Joshua Lapidis
Benjamin Life

Selection will be based on alignment, capacity, and community trust.

 How to Submit
Please send a proposal that includes:

Team bios & relevant experience
Timeline & milestone plan
Proposed facilitation methodology
Budget breakdown
Related work examples or references
Reflections on Regen Commons goals & values

Deadline: April 15, 2025
Email: gregory@regen.network
Telegram: @cpt_grog

 Key Resources
We strongly recommend reviewing these background materials:

[Brand Commons Legal Strategy Memo]
[Summary of Multi-sig Responsibilities]
[Regen Commons 1-Pager for ETH Denver]
[Regen Commons Tweet Thread]
[Regen Commons Discourse Forum]


 Why This Matters
Regen Commons is not just a DAO. It is a memetic, legal, and cultural coordination layer for the regenerative Web3 movement.
Help us build a legitimate, plural, and anchored foundation—and co-create a new model for governing decentralized cultural assets with integrity.

## Post 5 by Gregory0
*2025-05-13T16:42:30.950Z*

Regen Network’s tm is the trademark in question.  We’ve already negotiated with people over the use of the term “Regen” in the space covered by the trademark.  (specifically "Regen as used by Regeneration.org).  So Regen Registry, Regen Marketplace, Regen Token, Regen Coin, etc are all covered by that mark.  Essentially anything that can “cause market confusion” is covered by a mark like this.  I’d like to continue to reiterate: we are hoping to create a coherent commons to govern this mark for the larger community, not be engaging as an enforcement body.  If a community is coming together and wants to fully open the mark, that’s one possible outcome.  Another is to maintain the mark in order to build coherence and strong norms around usage, but as governed by a community and not a single business entity.

documents.title: The Legitimacy Paradox
documents.content:
# The Legitimacy Paradox


## Post 1 by Gregory0
*2025-03-04T17:50:07.644Z*

What creates legitimacy?  Where does “Regen Legitimacy” Come from.  How do we grow it, cultivate it, and design mechanisms to support it?
I wanted to share a little convo I had with my friend Claude the other day, after some back and forth with Xavier from Regen’s Unite and some more back and forth in the Telegram Coordination group:
Analysis of the Regen Commons Challenge from Multiple Disciplinary Perspectives
1. Collective Action Theory
Challenge: The trademark commons presents a classic collective action problem. While all participants could benefit from a trusted “Regen” brand with shared governance, individuals may resist contributing to its formation if they perceive others are getting unfair advantages or if they don’t trust the initial conditions. The current resistance suggests that potential participants haven’t yet been convinced that the collective benefit outweighs their individual concerns about power distribution.
2. Commons Governance (Ostromian)
Challenge: You’re facing a legitimacy hurdle in establishing the initial conditions of the commons. Ostrom’s principles suggest that successful commons require clearly defined boundaries and local adaptation of rules. The current resistance may indicate that either the boundaries of what “Regen” encompasses aren’t clearly agreed upon, or that stakeholders don’t feel they’ve had sufficient input in designing the governance structure from the ground up.
3. Institutional Economics
Challenge: You’re attempting to transform a formal institution (trademark law) into a new hybrid institution (decentralized commons). The friction arises because the transition requires stakeholders to accept the legitimacy of both the old and new institutional forms simultaneously. Critics may see accepting your invitation as implicitly legitimizing the traditional trademark system they ideologically oppose.
4. Transition Design/Theory
Challenge: You’re in the messy middle phase of a system transition, where the old paradigm (centralized ownership) must temporarily coexist with the emerging paradigm (commons governance). The paradox emerges because the tools of the old system (trademark law) are necessary to bootstrap the new system, creating internal contradictions that are difficult to navigate without triggering resistance.
5. Movement Ecology
Challenge: The resistance likely stems from competing frames within the broader regenerative movement. Some factions may prioritize radical openness and reject any form of enclosure (even temporary), while others recognize the strategic value of using existing legal frameworks as protection against co-option. These competing narratives create fault lines that make coordinated action difficult.
6. Memetics
Challenge: The “Regen” meme faces competing selection pressures. On one hand, protection through trademark prevents dilution; on the other, restriction potentially limits its spread. The paradox is that the meme needs both protection and freedom to thrive. Critics may fear that formal governance will stifle the organic evolution of the meme that gives it power.
7. Game Theory
Challenge: You’re facing what game theorists might call a “second-order cooperation problem.” The first-order problem (protecting the Regen brand) requires cooperation, but establishing the conditions for that cooperation is itself a coordination game with trust issues. Without sufficient trust in your intentions, potential collaborators default to non-cooperation, even if cooperation would benefit them.
8. Polycentric Governance
Challenge: The resistance may reflect confusion about which governance centers have legitimate authority over the “Regen” concept. Your proposal creates a new governance center (the Commons) that must establish its relationship with existing centers of authority (traditional legal systems, informal community norms, etc.).
9. Legitimacy Theory
Challenge: You face a bootstrapping legitimacy problem. The Regen Commons derives its initial legitimacy from your trademark ownership, but some stakeholders question that very source of legitimacy. They can’t accept the invitation because they don’t recognize your authority to extend it, creating a circular impasse.
10. Paradox Theory
Challenge: This exemplifies a “performing paradox” where contradictory elements must be embraced simultaneously. You must assert control to give up control, and critics must accept your authority to help dissolve it. Rather than trying to resolve this paradox, successful navigation may require holding both positions in creative tension.


## Post 2 by groweco
*2025-03-08T09:33:34.489Z*

Gregory0:

Rather than trying to resolve this paradox, successful navigation may require holding both positions in creative tension.


I think Claude gave us a good direction here. The question now is:
How can we sustain this creative tension while trust grows?
Perhaps what we need is an iterative process, where legitimacy is not granted but continuously cultivated:
loop
define_intentions  // Clarify shared purpose and alignment
get_consent  // Foster voluntary engagement and buy-in
build_in_public  // Create transparency and shared ownership
receive_signaling  // Listen to weak and strong signals from the network
improve  // Adapt based on evolving conditions
end
In complex transitions like this, legitimacy might not come from a single decisive act, but from an ongoing, participatory process.
What kind of signals should we be paying attention to?
How do we recognize when legitimacy is truly emerging, rather than just being asserted?
Maybe legitimacy is less about control and more about patterns of recognition that emerge over time

## Post 4 by m3metix
*2025-03-20T23:46:16.682Z*

These are good provocations from Claude. Though I feel some of this framing presents several limitations but that is the deliberative and discursive process 

The analysis positions the challenges as a tension between centralised control versus decentralised governance, creating a false dichotomy rather than exploring emergent possibilities.
It’s a static analysis as the disciplinary perspectives examine the situation as a fixed problem to be solved rather than a dynamic, evolving system with multiple possible pathways.
The framing overemphasises power dynamics and control while underemphasising the relational foundations necessary for genuine commons creation.
It seems these challenges rely on expert perspectives rather than integrating diverse ways of knowing, including lived experience and traditional ancestral wisdom.
The framing emphasises barriers and challenges without equal attention to assets, possibilities, and the emergent potential within the situation.

I’d say that rather than starting with governance structures or trademark laws, maybe the least wrong approach would be to first focus on building relational trust through:

Circle practices like creating small, trust-cultivating spaces where different Earthian stakeholders can share their hopes, fears, and visions for what “Regen” means to them.
Some deep listening by engaging genuinely with concerns about centralisation and co-option without immediately trying to resolve them.
Storying circles to uncover the deeper values and aspirations that unite different perspectives within the regenerative movement.

I feel it’s easy to get technocratic and down the path of sophisticated governance mechanisms, legal frameworks, and theoretical models that look impressive “on paper” but really fail to address the deeper relational foundations. When we rush to structure and formalise without first building genuine connection and understanding, we often create solutions that nobody feels ownership of or alignment with. The communing, sense-making, meaning-making and symmathesy matters. And it’s slow work.
I think the technocratic tendency is particularly tempting in commons work, where we might believe that the right governance system or technical implementation will solve our relational and kincentric challenge. I’ve been there and made that mistake many times. Probably continuing to do so. I also think the broader “regen” web3 and liminal web movement has been too. It’s the challenge of dismantling the masters house with the masters tools. Repatterning the old without re/cognising what is yearning to be born.
Trust grows through consistent care, and genuine communing precedes effective action. So a few questions I have are:

How might we create the conditions for genuine communing both/and in face-to-face in place and in cyberspace?
What specific practices could help create those “conditions for genuine communing” across different contexts?
How might the “small, trust-cultivating spaces” be designed to welcome diverse ways of knowing and being?
What rhythms and cycles might support this work - balancing between gathering, reflecting, and acting? Particularly affording for timezones and places on spaceship Earth…


the times are urgent; let us slow down.


## Post 5 by Techniq42
*2025-04-25T02:52:38.757Z*

This reflection on technocratic tendencies resonates deeply with my experience in physical commons building. The recognition that ‘trust grows through consistent care, and genuine communing precedes effective action’ mirrors what I’ve observed in developing community food systems and shared resource networks.
To address your thoughtful questions:
On creating conditions for genuine communing across physical and digital spaces:
In my work with regenerative agriculture networks and Burner communities, we’ve found that commoning emerges most naturally when centered around ‘boundary objects’ - tangible resources or challenges that multiple stakeholders care about but perceive differently. Food systems are particularly powerful for this - everyone eats, but different participants (farmers, distributors, consumers) experience the system differently. Creating spaces where these perspectives can interact around something concrete bypasses many theoretical disagreements.
On specific practices that create conditions for genuine communing:
We’ve had success with what we call ‘minimum viable commons’ demonstrations - small, tangible implementations of commons principles that produce immediate individual benefit while building toward collective outcomes. Examples include community blast chillers for food rescue, backyard growing systems with permeable sharing agreements, and mobile soil-building operations that connect waste generators with farmers. These create feedback loops between theory and practice, where governance emerges from doing rather than precedes it.
On designing trust-cultivating spaces that welcome diverse ways of knowing:
Our approach involves ‘graduated sharing’ - creating multiple entry points for participation that don’t require full ideological alignment upfront. Someone can contribute waste to a composting system without embracing a comprehensive commons philosophy, but through that participation, they begin to experience the benefits of commons-based resource flows. Their involvement can deepen organically as trust develops through demonstrated impact.
I see fascinating parallels between these physical communing practices and the challenges you’re describing in the digital commons space. Perhaps the legitimacy paradox becomes more navigable when digital governance concepts are grounded in tangible expressions that people can see, touch, and benefit from directly. I’d be curious to explore how these worlds might inform and strengthen each other.
